new_statements.quote: In both Orokolo and Toaripi, with words of two or three syllables, the stress is normally on the penultimate syllable. There are some exceptions, the most notable being with the nominative form of the personal pronouns: ara /ará/ I, are /aré/ 'he', 'she', 'it'; ere /eré/ 'they'. The stress pattern here has possibly been influenced by the object and genitive markers, the addition of which to a pronoun normalises the stress. [...] With words of four or more syllables, the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress has a minor stress, e.g. karikara /kàrikàra/ 'village'. The stress of the stem is repeated in reduplicated words, e.g. hirihiri /hírihíri/ 'dirty', hohorohohoro /hohórohohóro/ 'radiance'.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's penultimate primary stress and its 4- and 5-syllable patterns (1010, 01010: secondary two syllables before the penult). Refines it with the pronoun exception and with the reduplication rule, under which a 6-syllable reduplicated word such as hohorohohoro is 010010 rather than the catalog's 101010; Brown gives no non-reduplicated 6-syllable example, so the catalog's longer alternating patterns are not directly confirmed or denied. Statement is explicitly about Orokolo (and Toaripi) by the author of the Orokolo dictionary and the 1972 thesis.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (stated for words of two or three syllables, and as 'the main penultimate stress' for longer words). In words of four or more syllables a secondary ('minor') stress falls two syllables before the main penultimate stress. Reduplicated words keep the stress of each copy of the stem.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'With words of four or more syllables, the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress has a minor stress', e.g. karikara 'village' (4 syllables: secondary on syllable 1, primary on syllable 3). Only one minor stress is stated; nothing is said about further alternation in 6+ syllable non-reduplicated words.
new_statements.exceptions: Nominative personal pronouns are final-stressed (ara /ará/ 'I', are /aré/ 'he/she/it', ere /eré/ 'they'); adding the object marker -ro or genitive -ve 'normalises' them to penultimate stress (araro /aráro/, arave /aráve/, etc.). Final stress on the pronouns also distinguishes them from homographs with normal penultimate stress (p. xiii: the same diacritic marks are 'new' /are/ vs are 'he'). Reduplicated words repeat the stem stress: hohorohohoro /hohórohohóro/ (a 6-syllable word stressed 010010, not the strictly alternating pattern).
new_statements.identity_note: Brown's statements cover Orokolo proper (Western Eleman, the variety of the Orokolo village cluster and the Bible translation) and Toaripi (Eastern Eleman) jointly; he explicitly extends the Toaripi stress description to Orokolo (1973 p. 350) and states the rule for 'both Orokolo and Toaripi' (1986 p. xiv). No dialect of Orokolo (Muru, Aheave, Belepa/Keuru, Opao) is singled out for stress.

new_statements.quote: p. 350: 'In stress, juncture, and intonation Orokolo is in agreement with Toaripi.' — p. 307 (Toaripi): 'Stress: Words of two or three syllables usually take the stress on the penultimate syllable, e.g. haro /háro/ head, sosoru /sosóru/ firefly. There are some exceptions; e.g. faitora /fáitora/ now. Final diphthongs take the stress as though two syllables, e.g. mapai /mapái/ hear. [...] Where there are four or more syllables, there is a minor stress on the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress; thus karikara /karikára/ village. Compounds exhibit this same stress pattern: maeamariti /màeamaríti/ shame. Reduplicated words repeat the stress of the stem, e.g. sirisiri /sírisíri/ dirty, sosorusosoru /sosórusosóru/ radiance. There is often a reversal of the normal pattern with onomatopoeic words'

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's penultimate primary stress and 4/5-syllable secondary pattern; refines with the diphthong-as-two-syllables count, compounds, lexical exceptions and the reduplication pattern. The Orokolo statement itself is a one-line cross-reference to the Toaripi description ('in agreement with Toaripi'), so the detailed rule is Toaripi's, extended by the author to Orokolo.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Orokolo stress is stated to be identical to Toaripi's: primary stress on the penultimate syllable; a final diphthong counts as two syllables (so mapai is stressed on the a of -ai); words of four or more syllables and compounds carry a minor stress two syllables before the main penultimate stress; reduplications repeat the stem's stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes (via Toaripi): 'a minor stress on the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress', e.g. karikara /karikára/ 'village', compounds maeamariti /màeamaríti/ 'shame'.
new_statements.exceptions: faitora /fáitora/ 'now' (antepenultimate); nominative pronouns ara, are, ela, ere final-stressed, normalised to penult with -ro/-ve; final diphthongs behave as two syllables; onomatopoeic words often reverse the pattern (kekekeke /kekékeké/, hohohoho /hohóhohó/); reduplications repeat stem stress (sosorusosoru /sosórusosóru/ = 010010).
new_statements.identity_note: Brown's statements cover Orokolo proper (Western Eleman, the variety of the Orokolo village cluster and the Bible translation) and Toaripi (Eastern Eleman) jointly; he explicitly extends the Toaripi stress description to Orokolo (1973 p. 350) and states the rule for 'both Orokolo and Toaripi' (1986 p. xiv). No dialect of Orokolo (Muru, Aheave, Belepa/Keuru, Opao) is singled out for stress.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on primary placement: every opened source (Brown 1973 p. 350 via p. 307; Brown 1986 p. xiv) puts Orokolo main stress on the penultimate syllable, matching the catalog stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable). One detail differs from the catalog's strict alternation for long words: Brown states only one minor stress, two syllables before the penult, and says reduplicated words repeat the stem's stress, so a 6-syllable reduplication such as hohorohohoro /hohórohohóro/ (Brown 1986) or sosorusosoru /sosórusosóru/ (Brown 1973, Toaripi) is 010010, whereas the catalog gives 101010 for six syllables; no non-reduplicated 6+ syllable example is given, so this is a refinement (morphological exception), not a contradiction. Lexical exceptions (final-stressed nominative pronouns ara/are/ere, antepenultimate faitora 'now', onomatopoeia) are not encoded in the catalog. Brown 1986 prints karikara as /kàrikàra/ (two graves, apparently a typographic slip) where Brown 1973 prints /karikára/; the prose in both places gives the same rule. The listed work, Brown 1972, could not be opened, so nothing from it can be set against the others.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at Brown 1986: xiv in the PDF we hold, and independently corroborated in the held Brown 1973 (PL C-26) at p. 307 (rule stated for Toaripi with examples) and p. 350 ('In stress, juncture, and intonation Orokolo is in agreement with Toaripi'). (2) The deciding source is a dictionary introduction, but by the sole authority on the family, and it agrees with his 1973 sketch; Glottolog's actual bibliography (downloaded) lists no phonology article, instrumental study, or other grammar besides Brown's own 1972 thesis. The classification fixed penultimate primary stress with a secondary two syllables to its left is exactly what both held sources say; the only soft spots are (a) 'normally' plus a closed class of final-stressed nominative pronouns (and Toaripi fáitora), which does not threaten a fixed: penultimate syllable coding, and (b) iteration of secondary stress beyond one 'minor stres
